title: Quality Engineering
blurb: Build confidence with tests that detect real defects, and understand what coverage does and does not prove.

mustKnow.title: Test pyramid: when to change the balance
mustKnow.body: The test pyramid described by Mike Cohn puts many fast, focused unit tests at the base, integration tests in the middle, and a few slower, more brittle E2E tests at the top for important flows. These proportions are not fixed: when most code connects to a database or service, integration failures may deserve more emphasis, as in Kent C. Dodds’s testing trophy. Test each risk at the lowest layer that can actually detect it. Avoid an inverted pyramid, or ice-cream cone, dominated by E2E or manual tests.

mustKnow.title: Good unit tests: AAA and one behavior
mustKnow.body: Structure a test as Arrange (prepare data), Act (call the code), and Assert (check the result). Give each test one behavior and a name that states the condition and expected result, so a failure identifies what broke. One behavior can require several assertions, such as checking multiple fields of one returned object. Tests must run independently, without relying on order or state left by another test.

mustKnow.title: Test behavior, not implementation
mustKnow.body: Test inputs and observable results through a public interface rather than the order or count of internal method calls. Tests tied to implementation details break during refactoring even when behavior stays correct. This can discourage refactoring or lead teams to weaken tests until they no longer detect bugs. Exporting internal functions solely to test them is a common warning sign.

mustKnow.title: Test double: mock, stub and fake
mustKnow.body: Test doubles replace dependencies that are slow or hard to control, such as networks, clocks, or payment gateways. A stub returns predefined values; a fake is a simplified working implementation, such as an in-memory repository. A mock verifies calls and their arguments, which is useful for side effects such as sending email. Jest often creates all of these with jest.fn() and calls them mocks, but distinguishing their roles helps you choose whether to assert results or interactions.

mustKnow.title: Boundary values: bugs at the edges
mustKnow.body: Errors such as using > instead of >= or an off-by-one loop often appear only at a boundary, so testing values in the middle can miss them. Divide inputs into equivalence partitions and test values immediately on both sides of each boundary. For free shipping from 500 onward, test 499 and 500 rather than only 100 and 1000. Also consider zero, negative values, empty lists, empty strings, and null.

mustKnow.title: Linter, formatter and static analysis
mustKnow.body: Linters, type checkers, and formatters inspect code without running it. Tools such as ESLint, TypeScript, and Prettier catch unused variables, incompatible types, and—through typescript-eslint rules—unawaited promises faster than separate tests for each occurrence. Apply the same rules in editors, pre-commit checks, and CI so reviews focus on logic and design. These tools cannot establish whether business rules are correct, so they do not replace testing.

mustKnow.title: What coverage can and cannot tell you
mustKnow.body: Coverage shows which lines or branches ran during tests, helping you find untested code. It does not show whether the results were asserted: merely calling a function can increase coverage. A mandatory percentage can encourage meaningless tests. Use coverage, especially branch coverage, to find blind spots rather than to prove test quality.

mustKnow.title: Flaky tests: inconsistent results
mustKnow.body: A flaky test passes and fails without a code change, often because it depends on real time, fixed sleeps, shared state, test order, or an external network. Repeated reruns can train a team to ignore failures that indicate real bugs. Fix the cause by controlling the clock, using fake timers, or isolating each test’s state. If an immediate fix is not possible, quarantine the test with tracked follow-up work instead of relying permanently on retries.

mustKnow.title: TDD: Red, Green, Refactor
mustKnow.body: Write a failing test for the next behavior (Red), write the smallest implementation that passes (Green), then improve the code while tests protect its behavior (Refactor). Observing the initial failure demonstrates that the test detects the missing behavior. If it passes immediately, either the behavior already exists or the test is not checking it correctly. TDD works well for clear logic with fast feedback; exploratory work or a rapidly changing UI may call for tests afterward.

mustKnow.title: Over-mocking: green tests, broken systems
mustKnow.body: Mocking every dependency, including your own classes, may verify only that code makes the calls you expected. A mock can return a result that the real dependency would never produce, leaving tests green despite invalid SQL or a renamed field. Warning signs include mock setup longer than the test and failures after every refactor. Prefer mocking boundaries you do not own, use fakes when practical, and add integration tests against real dependencies, for example a database started with Testcontainers.

mustKnow.title: Performance and load testing
mustKnow.body: Load testing measures behavior at expected traffic levels; stress testing pushes beyond them to find limits; soak testing runs for longer to expose issues such as memory leaks. Inspect high-percentile latency (p95 and p99) and error rates rather than averages that hide slow requests. Results are useful when the environment, data volume, and usage patterns resemble production. Common tools include k6, JMeter, Gatling, and Locust.

mustKnow.title: Contract testing and mutation testing
mustKnow.body: Consumer-driven contract testing, such as Pact, records what a consumer expects from an API and checks that contract in the provider’s CI. It can detect changed fields without an E2E test spanning every service. Mutation testing, such as StrykerJS or PIT, makes small code changes and reruns tests; a surviving mutant usually reveals a missing assertion, unless it is equivalent to the original code. It measures fault detection more directly than coverage, but is slower, so teams often run it on changed code or periodically.

mustKnow.title: ISTQB’s seven testing principles
mustKnow.body: ISTQB gives seven testing principles: testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects; exhaustive testing is impossible; early testing saves time and money; defects cluster; tests wear out; testing is context-dependent; and absence of defects does not guarantee a useful system. Refresh tests and data as the product changes, and validate user needs as well as verifying requirements. Do not interpret ‘tests wear out’ as saying repeated regression tests are useless: the syllabus explicitly recognizes their continuing value.

mustKnow.title: Test levels versus test types
mustKnow.body: A test level identifies where you test: ISTQB lists component, component integration, system, system integration, and acceptance testing. A test type identifies what you test, such as functional, non-functional, black-box, or white-box testing. Types can apply at any level; measuring a function’s response time is a non-functional component test. Distinguish integration between components inside your system from integration with an external system, such as a payment gateway.

mustKnow.title: Confirmation testing and regression testing
mustKnow.body: Confirmation testing reruns the failing case to verify that the original defect is fixed. Regression testing checks that the change has not broken the same component, other components, or connected systems. After fixing a coupon calculation, confirm the previously incorrect case and run related checkout tests. Automate frequently run regression tests in CI, and use impact analysis to choose their scope.

mustKnow.title: Async tests: await or return the promise
mustKnow.body: Jest must know when asynchronous work finishes: return its promise or await it. Otherwise the test may finish before a promise resolves or rejects. Always await or return .resolves and .rejects assertions. With try/catch, ensure the test also fails if no rejection occurs, for example using expect.assertions(n) or storing the error and asserting outside the catch.

mustKnow.title: Setup, teardown, and isolated state
mustKnow.body: beforeEach and afterEach run around each test; beforeAll and afterAll run once for their file or describe block. Hooks inside describe apply to that block, and outer beforeEach hooks run before inner ones. A test that passes alone but fails with the suite often depends on state left by another test. Create or reset mutable data in beforeEach rather than sharing it at file scope or through beforeAll.

mustKnow.title: Defect reports: severity and priority
mustKnow.body: A defect report should let someone reproduce and fix a problem without follow-up questions. Include a concise title, the test object and environment, reproduction steps, expected and actual results, logs or screenshots, severity, priority, and status. Severity describes impact; priority describes the order or urgency of fixing it. They can differ: a distorted logo before tomorrow’s press conference may have low functional impact but high priority.

mustKnow.title: Decision table and state transition testing
mustKnow.body: A decision table describes outcomes determined by combinations of conditions: rows hold conditions and actions, and columns hold rules. Coverage measures the proportion of feasible rules tested; three independent boolean conditions create eight combinations. State transition tests describe event sequences that move a system between states, with coverage levels including all states, valid transitions, and all transitions. The last also attempts invalid transitions; use separate tests so one defect does not mask another.

# ตัวอย่างสมมติ: กฎส่วนลดของร้านค้า

is_member             T   T   F   F

mustKnow.title: Playwright: locators, auto-waiting, and assertions
mustKnow.body: Playwright automatically waits for an element to be ready before acting: a click checks that it uniquely matches, is visible, stable, unobstructed, and enabled. Prefer user-facing locators such as getByRole over selectors coupled to DOM structure. Use retrying web-first assertions such as await expect(locator).toBeVisible(); expect(await locator.isVisible()).toBe(true) checks only once and can be flaky. Keep each test independent of previous tests.

mustKnow.title: Snapshot testing: review the diff
mustKnow.body: Snapshot tests save serialized output in a text file and compare future output against it, making them useful for small, specific structures such as component output or error messages. Commit .snap files and review their diffs as part of the test. Control changing values such as time and random IDs, or use property matchers; Jest does not create new snapshots automatically in CI mode. Updating with jest -u without reading the diff turns the test into a rubber stamp for unintended changes.

mustKnow.title: Property-based testing with fast-check
mustKnow.body: Property-based testing defines relationships between input and output that must hold for all supported inputs. A library generates many inputs and shrinks a failing case toward the smallest counterexample it can find. Example properties include sorted output being nondecreasing with unchanged length, or decode(encode(x)) returning x. A general caution, not taken from the linked page: duplicating the implementation’s formula in a property can reproduce the same error and detect nothing.

mustKnow.title: Risk-based testing: prioritize by risk
mustKnow.body: When exhaustive testing is impossible, ISTQB recommends prioritizing by risk: the likelihood of a problem and its impact. Assess risk quantitatively by multiplying likelihood and impact, or qualitatively with a risk matrix. Use it to choose test levels, techniques, scope, and coverage depth. Newly written authentication code usually deserves more attention than renamed button labels; defect history also informs the assessment.

mustKnow.title: jest.mock hoisting and partial mocks
mustKnow.body: With babel-jest, jest.mock calls are hoisted before imports, so their factories cannot normally reference variables outside their scope. Jest permits names beginning with mock, but you must ensure those variables are initialized when needed. A factory that returns only some exports removes the rest; use jest.requireActual to preserve real exports and replace only selected ones. For different mocks in individual tests, use jest.doMock, which is not hoisted.

questions.prompt: Most of one service’s work is handling requests and reading or writing PostgreSQL. Its many unit tests mock every repository, but most production bugs involve invalid SQL or migrations that do not match the code. How should the team adjust its testing strategy?
options: Add unit tests to the mock repository to cover all types of queries.
Add an integration test that runs with real PostgreSQL, such as in a container.
Write E2E through the UI for every case of every endpoint.
Set a minimum coverage of 90% in CI for every PR to pass.
questions.explain: The bug is at the junction with the database, which is invisible to the mock. Therefore, more weight should be given to integration tests, which is the lowest layer that catches this bug. Adding unit tests to the mock repository will cause the test to continue to run green even if the SQL is incorrect. E2E in all cases is unnecessarily slow and brittle.

questions.prompt: This test fails in CI and only reports that the “order” is broken. What is the main problem with this test?
options: It has several expect calls; a unit test must always contain exactly one assertion.
It creates a real Order rather than a mock, so it cannot be a unit test.
It combines several behaviors, making a failure hard to diagnose.
It does not use beforeEach, making the test slow and hard to read.
questions.explain: Billing, coupons, and cancellation are checked under one name, so a failure requires inspecting the test, and later assertions never run. Split the behaviors into clearly named tests. Multiple assertions are fine when they check the same behavior.

questions.prompt: This test passes locally but sometimes fails on a busy CI machine. What addresses the cause?
options: Increase sleep to 2000 ms to allow enough time on slow CI machines.
Set CI to retry tests that fail automatically 3 times before reporting results.
Let startReportJob return promise and await instead of guessing the time with sleep.
Move this test to run last to prevent other tests from competing for CPU.
questions.explain: The test assumes the job finishes within 200 ms, which may fail on a busy CI machine. Wait for completion directly, or control time with fake timers. Longer sleeps make every run slower without removing the cause; retries hide it.

questions.prompt: You do TDD to add the rule “VIP members get 10% discount”. Write a new test and run it. It passes immediately even though you haven't edited the code yet. What should I do next?
options: Skip to refactoring because the test is already green.
Delete the test because a test that never failed is useless.
Implement the discount as planned and inspect the test afterward.
Check whether the test detects the new behavior or the rule already exists.
questions.explain: The Red step demonstrates that a test detects missing behavior. An immediately passing test may have an incorrect assertion or setup, or the rule may already exist. Investigate before refactoring rather than trusting a test that has never shown the expected failure.

questions.prompt: The team refactors checkout to round to satang only once at the end. Every customer-visible total stays the same, but the following test fails. What should change?
options: Change toHaveBeenCalledTimes to 1 to match the new implementation.
Assert the total returned by checkout instead of an internal call count.
Revert the refactor because a failing test proves behavior changed.
Mock roundToSatang with a constant result to avoid testing rounding.
questions.explain: This test is tied to internal calculation methods. So it breaks even though the results don't change. Changing the number to 1 actually makes it pass, but it's still brittle and will break again in the next refactor. You should check the results that the user sees, such as expect(checkout(cart).total).toBe(...)

questions.prompt: A ticketing system offers student prices from ages 13 through 19, inclusive. Which set best tests the boundaries?
options: 15 alone, because the midpoint represents the entire range.
1, 15, 50, and 99 to spread tests across age groups.
12, 13, 19, and 20 to cover both sides of each boundary.
13 and 19 alone, because the requirements mention them.
questions.explain: < and <= or off-by-one bugs appear on the edge, so you need to test both the values ​​within and outside the range on both sides of the edge. Sets 13 and 19 only test the inside side. If the code is incorrectly written as age <= 20, it still passes.

questions.prompt: Most PR comments concern spacing, import order, and unused variables, leaving little review time for logic. What should the team change?
options: Write a detailed style guide and have reviewers help enforce it.
Set formatter and linter to run automatically in editor, pre-commit and CI.
Added unit tests that check the coding style of each file.
Let one senior reviewer make all style decisions.
questions.explain: Work that can be checked by rules should be done by a machine. Because it's consistent, you don't forget, and you can fix it automatically. Reviewers can therefore concentrate on logic and design. The style guide that is given to reviewers still takes the same amount of time to review and each person can interpret it differently.

questions.prompt: Coverage of this function is 100%, but mutation testing reports that mutants changed >= to > survived. What does that mean?
options: No test distinguishes >= from >; add a case where total is exactly 500.
The tool is misconfigured because 100% coverage proves complete testing.
Change the code to > because the mutant passes the tests.
Add more test values between 100 and 1000 for denser coverage.
questions.explain: The changed code still passes, revealing that no test distinguishes behavior at exactly 500. Values away from that boundary cannot distinguish >= from >. Coverage records execution, not whether the boundary result was asserted.

questions.prompt: Orders calls a Users API maintained by another team. Users renames fullName to name and deploys; both teams’ tests pass, but Orders fails in production. What best prevents this?
options: Let Orders mock Users' responses in more detail in unit tests.
Add unit tests on the users side until coverage reaches 100% before deploying.
Conduct consumer-driven contract tests where Users' CIs are checked against Orders' contracts.
Have every team run E2E across every service in staging before every deployment.
questions.explain: The Orders mock encodes that team’s assumptions and stays green after Users changes the response. Contract tests check the consumer’s expectations in the provider’s CI before deployment. Cross-service E2E tests can also catch this, but are slower, more brittle, and depend on shared staging.

questions.prompt: A product-search API meets its latency target with an average of 120 ms in a load test, but some users report very slow searches. What should the team inspect next?
options: latency at p95 and p99 and error rate under the same load
Rerun the load test with a reduced number of simulated users to make the results more stable.
The median value is because it tolerates outliers better than the average.
It is considered passing because the average is within the target. Users who complain probably have slow internet.
questions.explain: Both the average and median cancel out the group of very slow requests. If p99 is several seconds, 1 out of 100 requests will wait that long even though the average looks good, so high percentiles and error rates need to be looked at together. Reducing the load makes the results look better but doesn't match the actual conditions.

questions.prompt: A set of 600 automatic regression tests ran every night for half a year. But features that the team fixes frequently still have new bugs leaking to users. Which conclusion is most consistent with the testing principles?
options: The original test set caught fewer new defects. Tests and data should be adjusted according to the changed parts.
Green every night means there are no defects left. The bug that was released is a changed requirement, not the fault of the test.
Automatic regression should be stopped entirely because running the same test over and over has no value.
You should run the same set of tests more often, several times per night, to catch more bugs.
questions.explain: The "tests wear out" principle states that repeated tests will catch fewer new defects, so tests and data must be adjusted or written more. But the documentation indicates that reruns are still useful in some cases, such as automated regression, so they are not deprecated. As for running more frequently, it doesn't help because the same test set still checks the same things.

questions.prompt: Several months of defect history show most customer-reported bugs in one tax module. Testing time before release is limited. How should the team allocate it?
options: Time is divided equally across modules so that it is fair and no part is left out.
Specially increase the testing time at the tax calculation module because defects tend to be concentrated.
Skip the tax module and test the other modules first. Because there are many bugs, it means that testing will never end.
Test only newly written modules. because the old module has been used
questions.explain: The defects cluster principle states that a small number of components often have the majority of defects, and old defect information is the input to risk-based sequencing. So you should invest there. Equal division appears fair but is not associated with risk. As for skipping it because there are a lot of bugs, it's the opposite of principle.

questions.prompt: The team tested all requirements in the spec and fixed all found bugs. But after the release, users complained that the steps didn't match their actual work and were too difficult to use. This situation corresponds to which idea?
options: Pesticide paradox: Rerun of the same test cannot detect new defects anymore.
Exhaustive testing is impossible: not every possible input and path can be tested.
Absence-of-defects fallacy: Passing all requirements does not mean meeting the user's needs.
Defect clustering: All bugs are clustered together in a single module of the system.
questions.explain: Checking that the system complies with the spec (verification) does not guarantee that the spec meets actual needs, so it must be validated, such as having real users try it or doing acceptance testing. The pesticide paradox refers to the effectiveness of repeated tests, which is not a problem in this case.

questions.prompt: The team writes tests that call the payment gateway of the external service provider in the sandbox to check that the requests and responses are as agreed upon. According to ISTQB's classification, what test level is it classified as?
options: Component testing to directly test our payment modules in isolation
Component integration testing: tests the connections between two pieces of code.
Acceptance testing because it uses data that is close to the real thing in testing.
System integration testing because it tests connections with external services.
questions.explain: System integration testing focuses on the connections between the system being tested and other systems and external services, and should be done in a near-real environment. Component integration addresses the connections between components within the same system. This is the most confusing choice.

questions.prompt: A developer fixes incorrect totals caused by overlapping coupons. QA reruns the previously failing case and it passes. What should happen before closing the ticket?
options: Run a regression test on areas that might be affected, such as price and checkout.
You can close the ticket now because confirmation testing has passed which means the resolution is complete.
Run the same case again dozens of times. Until you're sure it's not flaky before turning it off.
Test only the screen showing the discount. Because the user sees the results there and does not need to look at other parts.
questions.explain: Confirmation testing only checks to see if the original bug has been fixed. Regression testing checks to make sure the change doesn't cause any other negative effects. This must be done even if the correction has been made through confirmation. The option to close immediately is missed here.

questions.prompt: Which e-commerce defect is best described as low severity but high priority?
options: The payment page crashes every time a customer uses a credit card during a flash sale, causing the sale to fail.
Export feature for old reports that no one has enabled. Causes the entire system to crash when a button is pressed.
The brand's name is misspelled on the campaign page launching tomorrow morning. The system still works normally.
The language switch button is misaligned by two pixels on some phones, which hardly anyone notices.
questions.explain: Severity measures impact, while priority reflects urgency. A misspelled brand name on tomorrow’s campaign page has low functional impact but needs an immediate fix. A payment failure during a sale is high in both; a rarely used feature that crashes the whole system can have high severity but lower priority.

questions.prompt: Shipping rules depend on three boolean conditions: membership, reaching a spending threshold, and a free-shipping coupon. Each combination may have a different result. How many rules does the full unreduced decision table have, and how is coverage measured?
options: 3 rules, one rule, one condition and measured by the number of conditions that are fully tested
8 rules and measured by the proportion of possible rules that are covered by test.
6 rules because each condition has two values. and measured by the total number of tests
9 rules of three conditions multiplied by three values and measured by lines of code that are executed
questions.explain: The three true/false conditions give 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 combinations, and the coverage of the decision table is the number of possible columns that are tested. Divide by the total number of possible columns. Thinking additively or one rule per condition makes a mistake. Because the results depend on the combination of conditions.

questions.prompt: Orders have statuses: Created, Paid, Shipped, Closed, and can only be canceled before shipping. The team aims for "all transitions coverage" in addition to testing every correct transition. What else must I do?
options: Nothing: visiting every state already gives complete coverage.
Nothing: every valid transition already covers all transitions.
Attempt all invalid transitions in one test to save time.
Attempt invalid transitions, such as cancellation after shipping, in separate tests.
questions.explain: all transitions coverage covers all valid transitions and must also attempt invalid transitions. Trying one test at a time avoids defect masking, where one defect blocks the other. Combining multiple cases into a single test risks errors. Valid transitions are a weaker level.

questions.prompt: Async getUser should reject with "not found", but a bug makes it resolve to null. The test below still passes. How should the test detect this?
options: Await expect(e.message) inside catch so it waits for the result.
Use expect(() => getUser(999)).toThrow("not found") without await.
Use await expect(getUser(999)).rejects.toThrow("not found").
Increase the timeout to give catch more time to run.
questions.explain: When getUser doesn't throw, the code in the catch never runs, so no assertions are called and the test passes without checking. Resolve it with .rejects (if the promise succeeds, the test will fail itself) or add expect.assertions(1). As for adding await in the catch, it doesn't change the fact that the catch doesn't run. And toThrow without await doesn't work with async functions because it returns the promise that rejects instead of immediately throwing it. Even if the code is correct, the test will still fail.

questions.prompt: The second test below passes with test.only but fails when both tests run together. What is the cause and fix?
options: Jest always randomizes tests; configure file-order execution.
The count function is wrong on repeated calls; edit only production code.
Create the cart once in beforeAll to make tests faster.
The shared cart retains changes; create a fresh cart in beforeEach.
questions.explain: The first test mutates a file-level cart, so the second sees leftover contents only when run together. Creating a new cart in beforeEach gives each test the same starting state. beforeAll preserves shared state, and Jest does not randomize tests in an ordinary file by default.

questions.prompt: A component change makes snapshot tests fail in 14 files. A developer runs jest -u and commits every update without reading it. What is the problem?
options: No problem, because snapshots are created from real code and are always correct.
jest -u approves everything that was not intended, should read the diff first.
You should not commit the .snap file because it is automatically generated by Jest.
You should delete all snapshot tests and rewrite them with toBe.
questions.explain: Snapshot files are part of the tests and need code review. Updating them without reading the diff can accept unintended behavior. Commit .snap files to version control, as Jest recommends, after reviewing the changes.

questions.prompt: A developer adds a toMatchSnapshot test, sees it pass locally, but forgets to commit the .snap file. CI runs Jest with --ci. What happens?
options: The test passes and Jest automatically writes a new .snap file on the CI.
The test is skipped and is skipped until there is a .snap file in the repo.
test fails because CI doesn't write new snapshots for you, you have to commit the .snap file.
The test passes, but Jest warns that there is a snapshot that has not yet been saved to a file.
questions.explain: In --ci mode, Jest fails a new snapshot rather than writing it unless --updateSnapshot is explicitly supplied. This prevents unreviewed snapshots from being accepted automatically. Commit the reviewed .snap file.

questions.prompt: The dev wrote this code and Jest complained that the module factory of jest.mock() does not refer to variables outside of scope. Which one correctly describes the cause and solution?
questions.code:
const fakeMailer = { send: jest.fn() };
jest.mock('./mailer', () => fakeMailer);
options: jest.fn cannot be used inside a factory; write a normal function instead.
Move jest.mock after require because Jest always follows source order.
Use jest.doMock whenever a factory references an external variable; there is no alternative.
jest.mock is hoisted; use a mock-prefixed variable initialized before the factory needs it.
questions.explain: Hoisting moves jest.mock ahead of imports, so Jest restricts out-of-scope variables that may not yet be initialized. Names starting with mock are allowed, but you must still initialize them in time. Non-hoisted jest.doMock is another option, not the only one.

questions.prompt: This E2E test is flaky because the “Saved” toast appears about 300 ms after the click. What fixes the cause?
questions.code:
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'บันทึก' }).click();
expect(await page.getByText('บันทึกแล้ว').isVisible()).toBe(true);
options: Use await expect(page.getByText("Saved")).toBeVisible()
Add await page.waitForTimeout(2000) before the line that checks for toast to wait long enough.
Set the test runner's retries to 3, try rerunning the entire test when it fails.
Changed the locator to be a more specific and more stable CSS selector for toast.
questions.explain: isVisible() checks once and returns the value immediately, without waiting. For web-first assertions like toBeVisible(), it will retry until the condition is true or the timeout expires. A fixed number delay is still guesswork, and the runner's retry just hides the problem.

questions.prompt: The designer refactored the entire website's CSS class name, causing almost the entire E2E set to fail even though the screen works as before. Most locators are written as div.card > button.btn-x1:nth-child(2) . How should I adjust this?
options: Designers are prohibited from changing class names again because tests rely on these names.
Change to getByRole with the agreed upon button name or test id.
Switch to full XPath from root because it's more precise than CSS.
Cut the E2E count in half to reduce refactoring time.
questions.explain: A locator tied to a DOM structure or class will break when the markup structure changes even though the behavior remains the same. Playwright recommends using a locator that is closer to what the user perceives, such as a role or test id as a convention. Long XPaths are more fragile.

questions.prompt: The “Edit Profile” E2E test depends on a previous “Login” test leaving a session behind. It fails alone or in parallel. What enables independent tests and clear failure diagnosis?
options: Force the running order to always test login first. then turn off parallel running
Combine every step into one long test so that you don't have to depend on each other.
Set retry to test profile edits in case the session arrives in time.
Have each test log itself in beforeEach without relying on other tests.
questions.explain: Each test should be independent with its own storage, cookies, and data. This makes the results repeatable and easy to debug. Forcing the sequence solves the problem but causes one test to break and spread to many others. A single, long test, even without relying on other tests, combines so many behaviors that it's impossible to immediately tell which feature is broken.

questions.prompt: This property test passes even when sortNumbers returns an unsorted array. Which property detects the bug?
options: Check that all pairs of adjacent members are arranged in ascending order.
Increase the number of random rounds tenfold for greater coverage.
Verify that the result is always an array, regardless of the input.
Verify that sortNumbers does not throw on any random input.
questions.explain: The existing property checks only length, which unsorted output can preserve. Assert that adjacent elements are nondecreasing. More random inputs cannot compensate for a property that never checks ordering; checking only the array type or absence of errors is too weak.

questions.prompt: Two testing days remain before release. Changes include a rewritten payment module, new About-page copy, and monthly internal reports. What should risk-based testing prioritize?
options: Start with the part that is easiest to test first in order to get the highest coverage as quickly as possible.
Let's start with the payment module. Because the chance of being wrong and the impact are both high.
Arrange the menus in the app so you don't miss anything.
Allocate the time equally to achieve team equality.
questions.explain: Risk level comes from likelihood and impact. Newly written code has a high chance of being wrong, and mistakes involving money have a high impact. Therefore, you should get the most sequence and time possible. As for starting with the easy part, the coverage numbers are good but do not reduce the actual risk.

questions.prompt: The function below has only one test, discount(1000, true). What does coverage show, and what is needed for complete branch coverage?
options: 100% statement and branch coverage because every line runs.
50% statement and branch coverage; add tests for both cases.
100% statement coverage but incomplete branches; test isMember=false.
Incomplete statement coverage; add a test reaching the return.
questions.explain: A single test runs every line (statement 100%) but never goes to the if-false path, so it doesn't reach 100% branch coverage (actually runs 50%). The branch coverage covers the statement coverage, but not vice versa.

questions.prompt: A new file-import feature has sparse requirements and one day until delivery. Which additional testing approach is most useful?
options: Use session-based exploratory testing with a charter and time frame.
Wait until the specs are complete before testing. In order not to waste time testing the wrong thing.
Write detailed, fully documented test cases in advance to complete all cases before starting to run.
Only use unit tests because they run quickly and do not require the tester's discretion.
questions.explain: exploratory testing Design, run, and evaluate tests while learning the system. This is useful when specs are small or time is limited. Having a session with a charter and time box gives structure, while waiting for specs leaves no time to test.

exercises.title: Test shipping-fee boundary values
exercises.prompt: shippingFee(total) charges 50 baht, gives free shipping for totals of at least 500 baht, and throws for negative totals. Write at least four Jest unit tests, each checking one behavior by calling shippingFee directly. Cover both sides of 500, zero, and a negative total.
hints: Separate totals below 500, totals from 500 onward, and negative totals; choose boundary values for each group.
Use 499 and 500 for the free-shipping boundary, and -1 and 0 for the negative-total boundary.
Wrap throwing calls in a function: expect(() => shippingFee(-1)).toThrow(). Calling expect(shippingFee(-1)) throws before expect can run.

checks.label: Include at least four test cases
Test exactly 500
Test 499, just below the boundary
Test a total of zero
Assert the error with toThrow
Wrap throwing calls in a function passed to expect
Assert the returned value with toBe or toEqual

exercises.title: Test async welcome emails with stubs and mocks
exercises.prompt: sendWelcome receives repo (user lookup) and mailer (email sending) as dependencies. Write at least three async Jest tests: a user with an email returns sent: true and calls mailer.send with that email; a user without an email returns sent: false and does not call mailer.send; and a missing user rejects with "user not found". Use jest.fn() for stubs and mocks instead of real dependencies, and await every promise.
hints: Pass fresh dependency objects into the function rather than mocking the whole module. Reset them in beforeEach to avoid state leaking between tests.
repo.findById and mailer.send are async. Use jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(...) and await sendWelcome(...) in an async test.

Check no email with expect(mailer.send).not.toHaveBeenCalled(); check a missing user with await expect(sendWelcome(...)).rejects.toThrow("user not found"). Without await, the test can finish before the assertion.

checks.label: Include at least three test cases
Await async tests and stub the repository with a promise-returning function
Check sent: true with an email and sent: false without one
Verify mailer.send receives the user’s email
Verify no mailer.send call when email is absent
Assert a missing-user rejection with rejects, assertion counts, or a check outside catch
Await or return rejects/resolves assertions

exercises.title: Test delayed retries with fake timers
exercises.prompt: retry calls fn once, then retries up to retries times after failures, waiting delayMs between attempts. If every attempt fails, it rejects with the last error. Replace slow real-clock tests with fake timers: verify success on the third call after two failures; verify that fn is called once before delayMs and again when the delay expires; and verify rejection with the final error when all attempts fail. Restore real timers after each test.
hints: Enable fake timers in beforeEach with jest.useFakeTimers(), and restore real timers in afterEach with jest.useRealTimers().
Use await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(ms) so promise callbacks run during time advancement. The synchronous version does not let pending promises continue in the same way.
Attach const assertion = expect(retry(...)).rejects.toThrow("...") before advancing time, then await assertion at the end. Attaching it later can leave the rejection unhandled.

checks.label: Enable fake timers with jest.useFakeTimers()
Advance timers asynchronously with advanceTimersByTimeAsync or runAllTimersAsync
Restore real timers in afterEach (or afterAll)
Verify one fn call before the delay ends
Verify three fn calls
Assert rejection when all attempts fail
Avoid real-time setTimeout waits in tests
